newsitem.title: ITALY: Venice film festival draws to a close.
newsitem.headline: Venice film festival draws to a close.

text.p: The Venice Film Festival, which ends on Saturday night with the Golden Lion awards ceremony, wrapped up its screenings of new films with eagerly awaited works from Australian and New Zealand directors.

New Zealand-born Jane Campion's "Portrait of a Lady" and "Shine" by Australian director Scott Hicks were the culmination of dozens of films shown during the 11-day festival held at the Lido resort facing the lagoon city.
The two films were shown out of competition and were not among the 17 vying for the Golden Lion award, to be announced during a ceremony which begins at 7 p.m. (1700 GMT).
"Portrait of a Lady", an adaptation of Henry James's novel of the same name, is Campion's first endeavour since her 1993 film "The Piano" won an Oscar for best original screenplay.
The film stars actress Nicole Kidman as a young American woman who challenges the limits set on her by the closed expatriate community she lives among in Europe. John Malkovich also stars.
"I am proud to be a Jane Campion woman," Kidman told a news conference on Friday before the film was shown, saying Campion portrayed the strength and independence of women.

"Shine" is a powerful and moving film based on the life of Australian pianist David Helfgott, who won wide acclaim in his youth as a musical prodigy but whose promising career was cut short by mental breakdown.
"This film is about an artist going so far out on the ledge that he topples over, he is consumed by the music he is trying to express," Hicks told a news conference on Saturday.

He said he first got the idea of making a film about Helfgott when he saw him give a recital in Australia about 10 years ago, and gradually over the years won the confidence of the pianist and his wife and convinced them to make the film.
Hicks said Helfgott performed about 80 percent of the music in the film, which has been showing for about three weeks in Australia and will open in Europe and North America later this year.

Among the films competing for the Golden Lion award are Irish director Neil Jordan's drama "Michael Collins", World War Two drama "The Ogre" by German Volker Schloendorff, the comedy "Box of Moonlight" by American director Tom DiCillo, and the Nicaraguan political drama "Carla's Song" by Briton Ken Loach.
The festival also will present at the closing ceremony lifetime achievement awards to Italian actor Vittorio Gassman, French actress Michele Morgan and American director Robert Altman.

Altman, who got his big break years ago when his film "M.A.S.H." won an award at the Cannes festival, told a news conference that film festivals like Venice were important outlets for young directors.
"The main reason we're here is to discover new talent," Altman said. "If it's left in the hands of the bankers, everybody's head will be cut off."
